https://news.antiwar.com/2026/07/30/roma.text: Romania Starts Shooting Down Stray Drones From Ukraine War That Enter Its Airspace Romanian officials on Sunday claimed one of their pilots shot down a Russian drone in Romanian airspace on Friday, July 24. They claimed two more Russian drones were shot down over the weekend. In response, Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs demanded a Monday meeting with Russia’s ambassador to Romania, Vladimir Lipayev. They presented him with fragments of a “Shahed-type unmanned aerial vehicle commonly used by Russian forces.” They informed him that a Russian diplomat had been declared persona non grata and would have five days to leave Romania. Romanian officials claimed Russian drones have entered their airspace consistently since the war with Ukraine began. They said their policy had recently shifted from monitoring the incursions to shooting the drones down if this could be done safely, far enough away from civilians. In May, NATO and Romanian officials claimed a Russian drone hit a residential block in Galați, an eastern Romanian town near the border with Ukraine. Two people were injured; the first time stray Russian drones are claimed to have hurt anyone in the country. Ukrainian officials said the incident proved that Russia was “a real threat” to Europe. At the time, Russian President Vladimir Putin said the wreckage of the drone should be given to Russia so that it could investigate the matter fully. Russia and Ukraine have been at war since February 24, 2022. During the past four years, each side has innovated and escalated its drone warfare. Each side attempts to hunt down the other’s drone operators and jam the other’s drones. In May, a NATO fighter jet shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia. The speculation at the time was that Russian electronic jamming had sent the drone off course. Ukraine apologized, claiming it was an “unintended incident,” but did not specify what happened. The Romanian claims of encountering Russian drones would be consistent with their drones being jammed by Ukraine or otherwise malfunctioning. Russia has been waging drone warfare on Ukrainian shipping in the Black Sea and Ukrainian ports. However, on Tuesday, Russia’s Foreign Ministry called the Romanian accusations “ groundless ” and vowed to respond to its diplomat’s expulsion. In a statement posted on its website, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said: “We reject these latest unfounded allegations. These orchestrated incidents and the accompanying propaganda campaign are evidence of the Romanian leadership’s attempt to cover up the disastrous consequences of their irresponsible policy of supporting the Kiev regime.” The statement seemed to suggest Russia was claiming Romania had engaged in false flag incidents or simply fabricated the entire narrative. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: A composite of stolen the Renoirs: Young Woman ‌at the Well and Madame Colonna Romano Photograph: https://musees.cagnes.fr/en/oeuvres/madame-colonna-romano/ View image in fullscreen A composite of stolen the Renoirs: Young Woman ‌at the Well and Madame Colonna Romano Photograph: https://musees.cagnes.fr/en/oeuvres/madame-colonna-romano/ Art theft Artworks stolen from Renoir Museum on French Riviera in latest heist Thieves took four artworks but it is thought they dropped two in museum garden as they fled Jon Henley and Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.37 EDT First published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 03.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google French police are hunting two thieves who escaped with two Renoir paintings from a museum on the French Riviera after breaking in through a hole cut in its garden fence. Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, about 10 miles west of Nice, said the pair appeared to have been “well equipped and well informed” about the museum, which houses works by the French impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir in his former home. The theft early on Tuesday is the latest in a string of recent museum heists in France and across Europe, including the brazen break-in at the Louvre in Paris last October , when ⁠thieves stole crown jewellery worth €88m (£75m), including tiaras, a brooch, necklaces and earrings. Masson told the local broadcaster Ici Azur that the two thieves sliced through the museum garden fence with an electric knife or metal saw, entered the building through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames. View image in fullscreen The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, Bryan Masson, said his office estimated the stolen art was worth €9m. Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty Images Police arrived about five minutes after the museum’s alarm system went off at 5.48am, Masson said, which “forced the burglars to flee in haste and helped limit the scale of the theft”. Two of the four works taken were abandoned in the museum gardens during the getaway, the mayor, a member of the far-right National Rally (RN), said. His office estimated the value of the stolen works at €9m. The two stolen paintings were Young Woman ‌at the Well and Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano. Both were on loan from the Musée d’Orsay, in Paris. “They’re Renoirs … you cannot sell them like that,” Masson said. The paintings the thieves abandoned were both portraits: Portrait of Madame Pichon, and Coco Reading, a portrayal of Renoir’s young son Claude. The Renoir Museum was established in 1960 in the mansion where the painter ‌died aged 78 in 1919. It houses about a dozen of his paintings and about 40 sculptures, as well as photos, furniture and objects including his easel and wheelchair. View image in fullscreen Renoir’s study at the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer. Photograph: DEA/G Nimatallah/De Agostini/Getty Images Masson called for greater security for museums around France . “This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art,” the mayor said. An art theft expert, James Ratcliffe of the Art Loss Register, said thieves were increasingly targeting valuable artefacts. “Sadly, without further funding to improve museum security, we are likely to see an increase in the number of museum thefts,” he said. “Each time thefts occur, it draws yet more attention to the perception of these museums as relatively easy targets. That can only encourage some criminals to consider them as straightforward places to steal from,” he told the Associated Press. Europol, the pan-European police organisation, said last month robberies at European museums were becoming increasingly violent, with some thieves brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives. The Europol report suggested specialist property crime or art theft gangs, who usually avoid violence, were being replaced by “individuals who often have histories of involvement in other types of crime”, who were recruited through social media. The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the jewels they allegedly grabbed in the seven-minute heist have not been found. Two of the suspects have reportedly told police the mastermind behind the heist was disappointed by the haul and thought “they could have taken more”. Italian police recently recovered paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m stolen from a museum in March. However, last month four of the most important works by the Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters View image in fullscreen Safely on the tarmac, the truth of what happened on flight 1073 is still emerging. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters First Edition newsletter Andy Burnham Friday briefing: How we covered the flydubai incident as it unfolded In today’s newsletter: When a passenger plane plunges 17,000ft amid claims of terrorism, hijacking and geopolitical intrigue, Guardian journalists have to try and separate fact from fiction in real time Libby Brooks Fri 2 Oct 2026 01.45 EDT Last modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 01.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Shocking news of a cockpit stabbing. Graphic footage of bloodied crew members. Mid-air testimony from terrified passengers. This was the tenor of the heart-in-mouth reporting as the horrifying events unfolded onboard flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv: the early morning budget flight that plummeted 17,000ft in under two minutes before the courageous intervention of passengers and crew averted an apparent hijacking, potentially saving the lives of not just the 170+ passengers and crew on board, but many more. This morning, speculation and conflicting reports are continuing to emerge about this dramatic incident in the sky above the most geopolitically sensitive region in the world. So how does the Guardian report a swiftly developing story engulfed in misinformation, as accurately and responsibility as possible? I spoke to the reporters, bloggers and editors involved to find out. But first, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work. Northern Ireland | Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement , with Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”. US news | Tennessee’s governor has suspended all executions in the state and ordered an independent inquiry after a botched attempt to put a condemned inmate to death on Wednesday night. AI | When prompted, AI chat bots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women , a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith. Europe news | A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned. In depth: ‘It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening’ View image in fullscreen Assaf Regavim filmed the first widely circulated video from inside the cabin. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images International leaders have rushed to praise Smit Machchhar, the captain of flight FZ 1073. Bleeding heavily from multiple stab wounds, he somehow managed to release his cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower his co-pilot turned assailant, an Omani national, who had attacked Machchhar in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Other crew members were able to stabilise the flight and, just before 11am local time on Wednesday, the Boeing 737 Max made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia . All 174 passengers on board escaped serious injury. Yesterday, as internationally coordinated investigations continued, the attacker’s motives remained unknown. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement, while claiming the co-pilot had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal . Other senior Israeli figures have been more vehement, with ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, describing the incident as a “terror attack” . Two Israeli security sources later told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement. Saudi investigators detained the co-pilot upon landing and are cooperating with the United Arab Emirates , the US, Oman and Israel to determine his reasons and potential affiliations. William Christou , a Beirut-based reporter with the Guardian, tells me: “They’re examining whether it’s a terror attack, whether it had any previous planning or prior direction, and if it could be a lone wolf attacker, who was perhaps motivated by anti-Israel hate, but wasn’t necessarily linked to any larger organisation or state.” ‘The story changed moment to moment’ William began drafting his initial report as soon as he woke up to news alerts about a potential hijacking. The Israeli government originally minimised the incident, describing it as a fight between pilots, while another early report suggested the plane had to land because of a fight between Ukrainian and Russian co-pilots. “I was sifting through so much misinformation,” he says. “The story changed very quickly, and moment to moment.” Back in the UK, Oliver Holmes was looking at flight trackers. Now based at Guardian HQ, Oliver has reported extensively across the Middle East. What I didn’t know until we spoke is that he once trained as a pilot, which has left him with an enduring interest in aerospace and aviation. Flight tracking websites have transformed how we report in-air incidents, he tells me. “Before any government has made an announcement, these platforms can tell you something seriously wrong has happened.” Flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft rapidly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes, just as it reached to the Saudi-Jordanian border. Oliver suggests that investigators will look at whether this sudden and ferocious plunge was why the plane eventually landed with part of its tail missing. Oliver sent what he could interpret from the tracking data to his international desk editors, who asked him to work on a tick-tock piece – not, for once, a reference to social media, but an old-school print term for an article that sets out the hour-by-hour narrative of an unfolding news story. “It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening,” says Oliver. Eventually there came a flood of footage purporting to show images from inside the plane – but was it real? Each clip that the Guardian incorporated into our reporting had to be verified, particularly given the potential for AI-generated fakes. (The Guardian’s head of photography Fiona Shields is fascinating here on how we assess AI images.) ‘Netanyahu was trying to present himself as Mr. Security’ But this wasn’t just an aviation disaster. “It was taking place in this hugely sensitive geopolitical situation,” says Oliver. “The plane landed in Saudi Arabia which does not officially have diplomatic relations with Israel.” The budget airline itself, flydubai, had by now suspended all its flights to and from Israel, but warned against “premature speculation” while multiple governments, and Israeli officials in particular, were doing just that. This incident has occurred at a moment of extreme instability across the region, with the strait of Hormuz still closed as a result of the US-Israel assault on Iran and the resurgence of conflict in Yemen. It is also weeks ahead of knife-edge Israeli elections , with polls showing Netanyahu’s current coalition unlikely to meet the threshold needed to form a government but no clear path to power for his rivals. Just days ago, Netanyahu warned Israel faced an unspecified attack risk during the election period – an assertion greeted with cynicism by political opponents. The Israeli military subsequently confirmed they had no specific intelligence of an anticipated attack. “Most people interpreted that as Netanyahu trying to stir up his base by presenting himself as Mr. Security,” says William. Nevertheless, Netanyahu’s supporters consider him vindicated. On Thursday, William tells me, the Israeli foreign ministry started briefing diplomats that the flydubai incident was an attempt to drive a further wedge between the UAE and Israel, a relationship already strained after leaks suggesting Netanyahu was personally alerted to the 7 October attacks by the UAE president a week before it took place, something the president has denounced as “an absolute lie”. ‘These stories can be incredibly powerful’ It’s a challenging time to report a story like this, says Taz Ali , who led our live blog which covered the incident unfolding in real-time on Wednesday. “Readers are making connections with what’s happening in the Middle East in general, and you’re trying to answer their questions, first with very scant detail and later with a deluge of information, much of which is proved to be inaccurate.” Taz, who has a decade of experience in reporting on global events, knows the human drama of a potential hijacking immediately grabs reader’s attention. “Often those stories can be incredibly powerful, involve emergency landings, and sometimes they end in great tragedies”. And with the recent 25th anniversary of 9/11, the incident had an even deeper resonance. “Especially with the anniversary happening so recently, those memories would have been so raw in people’s minds when they came to this story.” What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen Burlesque legend Blaze Starr reigns over Baltimore’s bawdy ‘block’ of strip-clubs and grindhouses. Photograph: unknown A new Taschen book of images from the National Geographic ’s archives charts a century of dramatic change. And this fantastic gallery shows a tantalising selection, from the burlesque clubs of Baltimore to a blimp crossing New York Harbour. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team I loved our piece on when book clubs get dramatic, featuring werewolf smut, bad book choices, and infuriation when people don’t actually read the book. Poppy Elle Hunt’s piece about the evolution and cultural significance of human hair tackles many questions I never knew I needed answering. Case in point: what on earth is the purpose of pubic hair? Lucinda Guardian contributor Katherine Rowland went to Chicago for the United Astrology Conference and tells a captivating story about the battle over who gets to interpret the stars and how they should do it. Poppy Philip Oltermann’s interview with German artist and writer Philipp Ruch is a fascinating read. Ruch argues that “most of the theories we have to explain the rise of the Nazis don’t make sense – the data tells a far darker story”, one that could help us understand the rise of right-wing extremists today. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters Football | Wales ended their long wait for a Nations League win by beating Norway 2-1 in Cardiff, while Portugal maintained their perfect start with a 4-2 victory over Denmark in Copenhagen. Football | The United States is poised to host the first Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028, becoming the latest in a series of major Fifa tournaments staged in North America. Football | Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister. Race riots, organised crime and institutional politics bring it bang up to date. Read Jack Seale’s full review . Read Alexis Petridis’s full review . Film Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie (in cinemas now) | ★★★ ★ ☆ Alex Gibney’s documentary follows the celebrated author’s life up to and after the attack, but what shines through is Rushdie’s remarkable courage. Read Peter Bradshaw’s full review . Art Renoir and Love (National Gallery, London, from tomorrow) | ★★★★★ Grab your straw boater – and revel in the Impressionist’s light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushes. Read Jonathan Jones’s full review . The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: Guardian The Guardian splashes with “Welfare changes may axe disability benefit for young”. The Times leads with “Emergency diesel talks after Trump ultimatum” and the Telegraph says “Trump tells Europe to release diesel”. The Mail runs with “Labour frees first of 10 tidal waves of convicts”, while The i Paper has “Burnham leaving the door open to snap general election in 2027”. The Sun , on Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments, says “Own goal”. The Financial Times goes with “Global bond sell-off leaves US trapped in vicious loop”, and the Mirror leads on an interview with a survivor of the Manchester synagogue attack, saying “He stabbed me 3 times but I had to stop him”. The Latest Photograph: The Guardian US woman on death row survives two lethal injections in Tennessee A woman convicted of murdering a schoolmate 30 years ago has been taken to hospital after surviving two rounds of lethal injections in Tennessee. Christa Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in 200 years. Pike, 50, has spent three decades on death row after she was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. A last-minute appeal to stop the lethal injection was overturned by the supreme court, but the state governor, Bill Lee, has suspended executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. Lucy Hough speaks to the attorney and anti-capital punishment campaigner Clive Stafford Smith. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings View image in fullscreen Illustration: Ben Jennings/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Bodhana Sivanandan at Harrow chess club. She has said she wants to become an outright grandmaster ‘as soon as possible’. Photograph: Jaimi Joy/Reuters Eleven-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan has become the youngest ever ‘woman grandmaster’ at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan – while playing on a car booster seat so she could reach the board. Sivanandan, who lives in Harrow, was taught to play by her father when she was five. Within a year, she was beating him and by eight she had beaten the former British champion Peter Lee. If she reaches a rating of 2,500 in the next 11 months, she will become the world’s youngest ever outright grandmaster. She fits her chess career around school, but takes everything in her stride. “Now that I’m in secondary school there might be more homework,” she says, “but I should be able to manage”. Her ultimate ambition, she says, is simply to be the best chess player in the world. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work?
